Learning Mandarin. I love learning how the characters are constructed and the ways they're put together. It's as equally frustrating sometimes wondering why in the hell they made certain decisions though.

Copying this from what I posted elsewhere on the site....

  1. The way the language "works." Germanic / western languages are pretty happy to make a logical construction of "This is acting upon that." Chinese abandons this, and you rattle on some senseless prose you'd expect to find as part of William S. Burroughs' literary dialog, and miraculously the other person uses context to understand it.

  2. A big part of the aforementioned context is the context within Chinese culture. A significant portion of the language is made of up of inside jokes built on top of other inside jokes that chain back thousands of years, often rooted in Chinese history, literature, or mythology. In learning Chinese you learn a very rich culture spanning thousands of years, a billion people and their ancestors, and hundreds of nations past and present

  3. Continuing context, you can't take what's said at face value. There are many layers of meaning in Chinese and a person often uses these to express what they really mean. In English we rely a lot more on what a person actually says, but in Chinese you have to think about how the other person might feel, as nuanced in their word choice and which "inside joke" they used to communicate. It has really made me think of how we communicate with others.

  4. The characters / writing system. It's like one giant puzzle, and it's such a joy to figure it all out. Throughout it you can watch the language evolve. It's similar to how "knight" reflects the old pronunciation from pronounced to silent K, but the characters allow a lot more in-depth examination of these evolvings, and provide a lot more insight than roman characters allow for. The characters also interrelate to some degree, and you can watch the trends, relationships, and get a lot of other information from characters you can spend an entire life studying and understanding -- all of it a joy.

... which is why you only ever use ECDH with curve 25519 for key exchange in TLS or SSH. It's not like this is news. Server operators allowing DH without elliptic curves or allowing the NIST curves either have no clue what they are doing (and should not be doing it) or are actively malicious.

Here is a guide from a few months ago on how to set up your SSH config properly, but the part about key exchange applies to any protocol that establishes encrypted channels (such as TLS). Notable quote:

We have to look at 3 things here:

  • ECDH curve choice: This eliminates 6-8 because NIST curves suck. They leak secrets through timing side channels and off-curve inputs. Also, NIST is considered harmful and cannot be trusted.

  • Bit size of the DH modulus: This eliminates 2 because the NSA has supercomputers and possibly unknown attacks. 1024 bits simply don’t offer sufficient security margin.

  • Security of the hash function: This eliminates 2-4 because SHA1 is broken. We don’t have to wait for a second preimage attack that takes 10 minutes on a cellphone to disable it right now.
